blocks.x: Product fleets in the field managed as products: OTA updates that never brick, telemetry that earns its bandwidth, support APIs your service desk can actually use — and firmware attack surfaces treated with the same gates as your cloud.
A connected product is a promise your support org keeps
blocks.sub: OTA waves as launches, telemetry budgets and support-grade diagnostics

blocks.x: A connected product is a fleet you promised to keep working: the coffee machine in 40,000 kitchens, the charger in 200 supermarkets, the pump at 900 sites. The engineering is fleet product management — OTA with staged waves and rollback, telemetry budgets that earn their bandwidth, and diagnostics deep enough that support resolves cases before the customer finishes the call.
Security arrives by design: device identity, signed firmware, and the update path as the most-defended surface, because OTA is also the attack path.
Below: the failure modes that turn product fleets into liabilities, the reference architecture of fleet management, and the console that keeps firmware current safely.

nodes.label: Secure element
nodes.detail: Root identity in hardware — device keys generated in the SE, certificates chained to the fleet CA; an identity that cannot be cloned is the platform's floor.

nodes.label: Firmware & A/B slots
nodes.detail: Signed updates staged to the inactive slot, health-checked, switched on proof — rollback is automatic on watchdog failure.

nodes.label: Desired-state shadow
nodes.detail: Each device holds its desired state offline; the fleet plane reconciles on connect — connectivity gaps never corrupt configuration.

nodes.label: OTA orchestration
nodes.detail: Cohort campaigns with canary gates, soak clocks and automatic halt on health regression — 48k devices update in nine days without heroics.

nodes.label: Entitlement engine
nodes.detail: Feature flags per device per contract tier, synced to billing — the fleet is monetizable because the entitlements are machine-readable.

nodes.label: Product telemetry
nodes.detail: Usage and health streams feeding the roadmap — churn signals, feature adoption and failure modes, aggregated with consent.

nodes.label: Fleet security
nodes.detail: Anomaly detection on device behavior (unexpected egress, credential anomalies), revocation at the CA — a compromised device is one certificate away from contained.

widgets.note: Click nodes for the contract each layer carries. The secure element is where trust starts — everything else inherits from it.

A firmware wave is a product launch
blocks.sub: OTA discipline, telemetry budgets and support-grade diagnostics — the connected-product operating model

blocks.x: Connected products fail operationally when firmware is treated as a patch instead of a launch: unsigned images, estate-wide pushes, no revert path. The discipline runs waves like releases — signed images, staged rollout with canary cohorts, health monitoring against auto-revert thresholds, and a wave report that reads like a launch review. Device identity is per-device and rotatable (a fleet with one shared secret is one breach away from a recall), and the telemetry budget prices sampling against cost so the fleet reports what decisions need, not everything it could.

Support is engineered in: a diagnostics API that turns 'it's broken' into queryable state, telemetry-shaped support playbooks, and update success tracked across hardware generations — because the fleet is heterogeneous and the wave that works on gen-3 may strand gen-1. The console reads fleet currency (who is on which firmware, which devices stopped reporting), and the support desk reads the same console, which is the point.

items: Signed, staged, monitored, reversible — with a wave report per release.
Rotatable credentials; no fleet-wide shared secrets.
Sampling shaped by decisions, enforced against the budget.
Queryable device state instead of 'it's broken' tickets.
What makes a firmware wave a "product launch"?

Same discipline: staged rollout with auto-revert, support briefed before the wave, telemetry watched for regression. A firmware wave that reaches a million devices without this is a product recall in waiting.
How do you handle failed updates in the field?

Auto-revert is the default: devices that fail health checks after update roll back to the last signed image, and the console shows revert counts per wave — a wave with unexplained reverts pauses by policy.
Can you manage mixed device generations?
Yes — per-line targets differ honestly: legacy line D carries 97.5% uptime and 80% currency targets because its hardware budget is real, and the defaults table prices the deviation of demanding more.
How does support see what the customer’s device sees?

The support desk reads the fleet plane: device state, firmware version, last update outcome and diagnostics. A 9–12 minute resolution target is credible only when support sees the same truth the device reports.
The fleet plane, the console with currency as the headline, the wave gates and the firmware-security overlay — operations runs the fleet as a product, not as a cost center.

blocks.x: Ask what percentage of your fleet runs current firmware — and what updating the rest would risk. The diagnostic will wire signed waves with auto-revert and make currency boring.
